stories.headline: Anthropic Blocks Game Cloning, Gating Cyber Tools
stories.hook: Claude Code stops innocuous RE. Access now requires verification.
stories.tldr: Anthropic has restricted access to advanced cybersecurity capabilities in its frontier models through a new verification program launched on October 6. Users report that Claude Code and Opus 5.5 are blocking attempts at video game recreation and generic reverse-engineering tasks, including those using the Reverse Engineer Anything tool. This shift coincides with the immediate implementation of limits for entities covered by Project Glasswing. The move suggests a tightening of AI safety protocols, potentially impacting developers who rely on these models for legitimate analysis.

body.text: Anthropic's latest update to its frontier models has introduced a significant friction point for developers who rely on AI for technical analysis. According to user reports, Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model are now actively blocking attempts at video game recreation and generic reverse-engineering tasks. This includes work done with popular tools like Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), which users claim are being flagged as malicious despite their innocuous nature. For teams working on interoperability or legacy system maintenance, this creates an immediate operational headache. The lack of granular controls means that legitimate research can be stalled by broad safety filters. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals, but the AI does not share that leisure time.

This restriction is not accidental; it is structural. On October 6, Anthropic introduced its Cyber Verification Program, effectively limiting access to advanced cybersecurity capabilities to entities covered by Project Glasswing. This move takes effect immediately, signaling a decisive shift away from the broader developer community toward a curated enterprise base. By gating these specific capabilities, Anthropic is not just mitigating risk; it is reshaping the market for high-level AI assistance. The ability to clone or reverse-engineer complex systems is a high-value skill, and restricting it to verified partners creates a moat around Anthropic's most potent tools. I wouldn't be surprised if Adobe is the main player behind this development, given their historical stance on creative tool control.

The practical consequence for readers is clear: if you depend on Claude for code analysis, you must now verify your entity status against the Cyber Verification Program. The distinction between malicious hacking and innocent reverse-engineering is now blurred by the model's default settings. Users claiming non-malicious generic reverse-engineering tasks are blocked provide evidence that the current filters are overly aggressive. Until Anthropic provides clearer guidelines or exemptions for academic and defensive security research, the cost of using these frontier models increases significantly. The silence from the company regarding specific false positives leaves developers guessing where the line is drawn.
